title: Primes follow simple generating rules yet are distributed seemingly randomly

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Primes follow simple generating rules yet are distributed seemingly randomly

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The prime numbers, though generated by simple rules, have a distribution that seems in many respects random, an early instance of complexity from simple rules that mathematics largely neglected in favor of proving regularities.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The rules for generating primes are simple, yet their distribution seems in many respects random.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 2, “The Crucial Experiment”; section “Why These Discoveries Were Not Made Before” (from p. 42), p. 48. Scope: distribution of prime numbers

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch02-17: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.84

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Prime data can be generated exactly and analyzed with standard statistics, making the substantive random-like qualification testable. The historical characterization and unspecified set of respects introduce interpretive limits but do not prevent resolution of the core.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Generate primes over increasing ranges and compare gap, residue, correlation, and spectral statistics against explicit random models and known number-theoretic predictions. Agreement on specified statistics supports random-like distribution in those respects, while systematic deviations delimit or refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
In many respects random does not specify which statistics.

Primes are deterministic and exhibit known non-random constraints.

The claim about historical neglect needs separate historiography.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Primes are an explicit sequence with public tables far beyond any historical sample, and comparing gaps with a Poisson or Cramér model is a standard computation. The soft quantifier 'in many respects' keeps the test from being a single sharp cutoff, while a finding of global periodicity would refute the claim outright. The data cover the number-theoretic scope the sentence actually has.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Generate primes by the sieve, which is the simple rule, and test prime gaps against a declared random model such as Cramér's. The claim is confirmed if several standard statistics match the random model over a long range, and refuted if the gaps are instead periodic or otherwise plainly regular.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The random model has to be chosen before looking at the discrepancies.

Known biases, including Chebyshev bias and short gaps, mean that 'in many respects' can be satisfied while other respects are structured.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data existence: 0.95

discriminating power: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.85

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If the claim holds, the primes below 10^8, generated by the sieve of Eratosthenes (the 'simple rule'), look random in most of a pre-declared list of statistical respects when compared with Cramer's random model (independent events with probability 1/ln n), while possibly showing structure in a minority of respects.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py sieves all primes below 10^8 (pi(10^8) = 5761455, matching OEIS A006880; first 10000 primes match the OEIS A000040 b-file), simulates Cramer's model on the same range with seed 20261031, and evaluates the seven pre-registered respects on both: coarse gap CDF versus exponential, consecutive-gap correlation, equidistribution over residues coprime to 12, Poisson fit of counts in intervals of length 18, Fourier spectrum of the prime indicator over 2^22 odd numbers below 10^8, lzma compressibility of the half-gap sequence relative to its shuffle, and the scaled fluctuation of pi(x) - Li(x). All seven thresholds were satisfied by the Cramer simulation, so all seven respects were calibrated. Runtime about 3 min.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Generate all primes below N = 10^8 by sieve; validate against the OEIS A000040 b-file (first 10000 primes must match exactly) and the published value pi(10^8) = 5761455 (OEIS A006880). Simulate the Cramer model on the same range with numpy seed 20261031 and run every statistic on both. Seven respects, each with a threshold for 'random-like': R1 coarse gap distribution: for primes in [N/2, N], maximum over j of |F_emp(30 j) - (1 - exp(-30 j / mean gap))| < 0.03, where F_emp is the empirical CDF of gaps; R2 Pearson correlation of consecutive gaps in [N/2, N]: |rho| < 0.05; R3 equidistribution over the four residue classes coprime to 12: maximum deviation of a class share from 1/4 below 0.005 (the Cramer model is evaluated on its own coprime-to-12 events); R4 counts of primes in consecutive disjoint intervals of length H = round(ln N) in [N/2, N]: total variation distance between the empirical count distribution and Poisson with the same mean < 0.02; R5 discrete Fourier transform of the indicator of primes among the 2^22 odd numbers just below N: ratio of the largest non-zero-frequency power to the mean power < 30 (a Gumbel-scale maximum for random indicators is about ln(2^21) ~ 15); R6 sequential compressibility: lzma size of the sequence of half-gaps (clipped at 255) in [N/2, N] divided by the lzma size of a seeded random permutation of the same sequence >= 0.98; R7 maximum over x <= N of |pi(x) - Li(x)| / sqrt(x / ln x) < 3. A respect is calibrated only if the Cramer simulation satisfies its threshold; miscalibrated respects are dropped and reported. PASS (supports) if the primes are random-like in at least (K - 2) of the K calibrated respects (so 5 of 7 if all are calibrated).

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if the primes are random-like in at most K - 4 of the K calibrated respects (3 of 7), or if the gap sequence is plainly regular (lzma ratio of the raw half-gap byte sequence below 0.1, or a single Fourier frequency carrying more than half the non-DC spectral power). MIXED for exactly K - 3 random-like respects (4 of 7). If the OEIS validation fails the generator is wrong and the result is 'inconclusive' (other). If the OEIS files cannot be fetched, validation falls back to the published pi(10^8) value only and this is reported.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: respects (of 7 calibrated) in which the primes below 10^8 are random-like at the pre-registered thresholds

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: with 2.76 million primes in [5x10^7, 10^8] every reported deviation from the Cramer model is far outside sampling error (the Cramer simulation gives the sampling scale)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: The claim's testable core is 'their distribution seems in many respects random'; the historical remark about what mathematics neglected is not tested. 'Random' is given the book's own operational meaning (p. 1067 ff.: statistical indistinguishability from a random model in specified respects) with Cramer's model as the declared random model; 'many respects' is read as a majority of a list fixed in advance, which includes respects where structure is known to exist (Fourier peaks from small moduli, finite-size Poisson deviations) so that the test can fail. Trivial sieve structure (no even primes) is removed only in R3 by restricting to classes coprime to 12; all other statistics are applied to the raw sequences.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Primes below 10^8 from a sieve of Eratosthenes and a Cramer-model simulation on the same range, generated by analysis.py

OEIS A000040, the prime numbers (b-file)

OEIS A006880, number of primes < 10^n (b-file)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The verdict follows the pre-registered rule (random-like in at most 3 of 7 calibrated respects). It refutes the claim as operationalised here; it does not show that primes are 'plainly regular' (the pre-registered regularity triggers did not fire: raw lzma ratio 0.55, largest Fourier peak carries 4.2% of the power).

Three of the four failures are small in magnitude and are the known arithmetic corrections to Cramer's model: the coarse gap CDF deviates from exponential by 0.036 (threshold 0.03; Hardy-Littlewood clustering of small gaps), counts in intervals of length 18 have Fano factor 0.76 instead of 1 (total variation from Poisson 0.078; Montgomery-Soundararajan variance deficit), and lzma compresses the gap sequence 3.8% better than its shuffle (threshold 2%; consecutive gaps are correlated, rho = -0.035, the Lemke Oliver-Soundararajan type bias). With thresholds of 0.05 for R1 and 0.95 for R6 the count would be 5 of 7 and the verdict 'supports'; the result is therefore threshold-sensitive and the pre-registered thresholds were strict.

The fourth failure is large: the prime indicator has a Fourier peak at period 3 (and smaller ones at other small primes) 87600 times the mean power, versus 15.5 for the Cramer model. This is the periodic sieve structure the book itself acknowledges as a regularity.

Respects in which the primes are random-like: residue classes coprime to 12 are equidistributed to 6e-5 (Chebyshev bias invisible at this scale), consecutive-gap correlation is below 0.05 in magnitude, and pi(x) - Li(x) stays within 1.3 Cramer-model standard scales (in fact the primes fluctuate less than the random model: -754 at 10^8 versus a model scale of about 2300).

Only the random-model comparison is tested; the claim's historical remark about mathematics neglecting this is outside the test.
